26.Ld Counsel for defendant had vehemently contended that the  present suit is not maintainable inasmuch as the suit property  has not been specifically identified by the plaintiff.
It was  submitted that order VII Rule 3 CPC makes it mandatory that  in a suit for possession, the details, including description of  the property have to be correctly and completely mentioned.
In the present case, the discrepancy firstly qua the actual area  of the property has also arisen.

In the plaint, the area of the  suit property has been mentioned as 80-85 sq yards, whereas  a perusal of the cross-examination of the PW-2 Smt Safia  reveals that the area of the suit property varies from 200 sq  yards to 100 sq yards.

In this context, it would be apt to refer  to the testimony of PW-2 Smt Safia elicited in her cross-  examination:
 "Court Question: Did you reside in suit property  after its purchase by you and for what period?

Further, whether the property is House no 28 or House no 58 Mohd. Akil vs Yunus on 4 February, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/27697725/
8  has also not been clarified.
In the cross-examination of PW-2  Smt Safia, she had admitted that no proof of document qua  dispossession of ownership of either House no 28 or House  no 58 was filed.

In this context, she averred as thus:
 "When I purchased the property, the house  numner of the property was 28, however after the  Residential Welfare Association was formed they  allotted the number 58 to the said house.
It is  wrong to suggest that house no 58 was not  allotted to house no 28 andthey both are different  properties.
I have not filed any proof of document  which shows my possession or ownership over  house no 28 or house no 58 on judicial record.
My father might have filed it."
28. The above revelation also assumes significance in view of  the fact that the assertion of RWA alloting number 58 to the  said house has also not been proved by the plaintiff.
It is trite  law that in case the suit property has not been described  correctly, the suit would not succeed.

In this context, it would  be apt to reproduce the relevant extracts of Mary Pushpam  (supra) wherein it was laid down as thus:
 "22.
In order to test the above agreement, we  carefully examined the judgement of the Trial  Court as also the First Appellate Court.
What is  discernible is that nowhere it is recorded the  actual boundary or the measurements of the  property in possession of the mother of the  appellant (defendant therein).

The respondents- plaintiff therein had based her case on the ground that they had purchased 8 cents of open piece of land and the defendant therein had raised construction over some adjoining land, CS DJ 5568/2016 Page. 14 of 21 Mohd Akil Vs Yunus and had trespassed over part of her purchased land as such decree of possession be granted.
23. We are unable to appreciate the said argument of the respondents.
Suit for possession has to describe the property in question with accuracy and all details of measurement and boundaries.
This was completely lacking.
A suit for possession with respect to such a property would be liable to be dismissed on the ground of its identifiability.
Further, it may be noted that if the construction by the defendant were not made over 8 cents of purchased land, then the plaintiff therein would not have a claim to possession of the same.

The argument thus has to be rejected not only on facts but also on legal grounds as discussed above."
29.Therefore, on this score also the suit of the plaintiff cannot succeed.

30.It is also the mandate of Section 6 of Specific Relief Act that the person who is claiming to be dispossessed without his consent, of immovable property, has to first assert and prove that he was in possession of the said suit property.

In the present case, the plaintiff has filed unattested photocopies of following documents:
Mohd. Akil vs Yunus on 4 February, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/27697725/
9 1.
Election ID card of plaintiff 2. Electricity Bill of BSES 3. passbook of Gas connection 4. Passbook of Syndicate Bank 31.
The above documents have not been proved by the plaintiff witness inasmuch as the documents were not tendered by way of evidence of the plaintiff.

Further, the documents on which CS DJ 5568/2016 Page. 15 of 21 Mohd Akil Vs Yunus the plaintiff placed reliance on to establish possession, are mere photocopies and the said photocopies have not been proved as per the Indian Evidence Act.
32.Even if the claimant wanted to prove the existence and execution of a document by secondary evidence, it was first required of him to prove the existence of one of the several situations mentioned in Section 65 of the Evidence Act and thereafter to prove the document by secondary evidence of the form and the kind permitted in that situation.
Without fulfilling this twin task, no document can be said to have been proved by secondary evidence.
The claimant has failed to lead foundational evidence qua the fact that the originals are lost or destroyed etc before leading secondary evidence.

33. At this juncture it would be apt to refer to the following extracts of Jail Prakash Aggarwal vs State 2017 SCC OnLine Del 6478, wherein the Hon'ble Court held as thus:
22.

entities.text: Jail Prakash Aggarwal vs State 2017 SCC OnLine Del 6478
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Thus, the person wanting to prove the existence and execution of a document by secondary evidence, before doing so, is first required to prove the existence of one of the several situations in which Section 65 permits proof of a document by secondary evidence and thereafter prove the document by secondary evidence of the form and the kind permitted in that situation.
Without fulfilling this twin task, no document can be said to have been proved by secondary evidence.

Such task can be performed only while leading evidence and the Court, only at the time of appreciating such evidence and which generally is at the time of final arguments, can hold whether a situation in which Section 65 permits secondary evidence has been proved to CS DJ 5568/2016 Page. 16 of 21 Mohd Akil Vs Yunus exist and if so, whether the document has been proved by secondary evidence.
No such finding can be returned on an application and without leading evidence.

The petitioner thus cannot take any advantage of the orders dated 22nd September, 2006 and 4th August, 2015 supra allowing the applications of the petitioner to prove the documents by secondary evidence.
In fact, the applications were misconceived as no permission for proof of a document by secondary evidence which is permitted by Evidence Act itself, is required.

It is for this reason that it needs to be examined on appreciation of the evidence led by the petitioner, whether the petitioner has proved Mohd. Akil vs Yunus on 4 February, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/27697725/
10 before this Court existence of any of the situations mentioned in Section 65 in which secondary evidence is permitted to be led.
Without the petitioner proving the existence of such situation, the question of proving the document by secondary evidence does not arise.

This is what is meant by "laying the foundation for leading secondary evidence".
34.
In the present case, the plaintiff has not been able to establish that the aforementioned documents are covered under the situations mentioned in Section 65 of the Indian Evidence Act.
35. Thus, the documents adduced on record by the plaintiff are inadmissible in evidence.

On the other hand, the defendant adduced and proved on record the following documents which bear the address of the defendant as House no 58, Gali no 1 Bapu Colony, Mandi Pahari, New Delhi, as per law:
CS DJ 5568/2016 Page. 17 of 21 Mohd Akil Vs Yunus (a) Ex DW1/1 viz. Copy of monthly payment receipt issued by RWA dated 06.03.2016 in favour of Kamar Jahan w/o defendant,
(b) Ex DW1/2 viz. copy of voter iD card of Kamar Jahan w/o defendant (c) Ex DW1/4 Copy of birth certificate of Sarukh Khan grand son of defendant.
36.
The above said documents reflect that the defendant was in possession of house no 58, Gali no 1 Bapu Colony, Mandi Pahari, New Delhi, and not the plaintiff herein.

37. In view of the above, the plaintiff has not been able to demonstrate that he was in possession of suit property and therefore all the four issues are hereby decided against the plaintiff and in favour of defendant.
v. Issue no 4a: Whether the present suit is barred by law of limitation ?
38.
A perusal of the plaint reveals that the date of dispossession has not been mentioned by the plaintiff.

The plaintiff has only averred that on 16.05.2013 when he reached his house for keeping an eye on his house, then it was found that the locks of his house were broken and the defendant Yunus along with his wife and one Mansoor were found sitting in the house after breaking upon the locks of the door of the house.

This date of 16.05.2013, as rightly pointed out by the Ld Counsel CS DJ 5568/2016 Page. 18 of 21 Mohd Akil Vs Yunus for defendant, is the date of knowledge of dispossession inasmuch as in the plaint itself, the plaintiff has mentioned that three years ago, all the family members of the plaintiff had fled away from the house in order to save their lives as Abdul Sattar and his sons and sister Smt Noori got furious and invaded the house of the plaintiff and his daughter Smt Safia.
Thus, as per the plaintiff itself, the date of dispossession was somewhere in the year 2010.

Mohd. Akil vs Yunus on 4 February, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/27697725/
11 39.It
is trite that in terms of Section 6 of Specific Relief Act, the plaintiff has six months limitation period to institute the suit on the basis of dispossession.

At this juncture, it would be apposite to refer to Section 6 of Specific Relief Act:
"6. Suit by person dispossessed of immovable property.--
(1)If any person is dispossessed without his consent of immovable property otherwise than in due course of law, he or any person claiming through him may, by suit,
recover possession thereof, notwithstanding any other title that may be set up in such suit.
(2)No suit under this section shall be brought-- (a)after the expiry of six months from the date of dispossession; or (b)against the Government."
40. Thus, the above provision of law makes it explicit that the terminus a quo is the date of dispossession and not the knowledge of dispossession.

This proposition gets fortified upon a perusal of following extracts of Indraprastha Cold Storage (supra) wherein it was held as thus:
CS DJ 5568/2016 Page. 19 of 21 Mohd Akil Vs Yunus 23.
It has already come on record that plaintiff has failed to prove as to on which date it was dispossessed from the suit property.
The contention of the plaintiff is that it has come to know about its dispossession from the suit property on 04.02.2016 when its official visited the suit premises.
However, as per Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, there is nothing mentioned about the knowledge of dispossession and it specifically speaks about the date of dispossession.

It is further added that plaintiff itself has moved application under Order VI rule 17 CPC for treating the present suit from one under Section 6 of Specific Relief Act to a suit for possession under the general law.
It is further pertinent to mention here that vide order dated 22.11.2021, said application was dismissed.

Further,
it is contended on behalf of the plaintiff that proceedings under DRC Act were pending against the sub tenants.
It is further the case of the plaintiff that sub tenants in connivance with the defendant company had handed over the possession of the suit premises to the defendant.

Thus, the sub tenants, whomsoever they may be, would be the best persons who could have come and state about the actual circumstances under which they had handed over the possession of suit premises to the defendant.
Hence, sub tenants in the present case were proper and necessary parties.
It is the case of the plaintiff that he has come to know about his dispossession from the suit property on 04.02.2016 when its official visited the suit premises.
Present suit has been filed by the plaintiff on 22.03.2016.
It has already been observed, as above, that no suit can be filed under section 6 of Specific Relief Act after the expiry of six months from the date of dispossession.
It does not say anything about knowledge of dispossession.

The plaintiff has relied upon G. Gururajan and Ors. Vs. P.M.
Duraisamy, MANU/TN/ 1160/1998.

12 when they have vacated the premises.

Apparently, no date of dispossession has been mentioned by the plaintiff and present suit has been filed on 22.03.2016, thus, it is not proved on record that present suit has been filed within period of limitation satisfying the ingredients of Section 6 of Specific Relief Act.
Accordingly, all these issues are decided against the plaintiff and in favour of the defendant."

41.This Court is thus inclined to concur with the submissions of Ld Counsel for defendant, and it is hereby held that the suit is barred by limitation as the same was filed on 03.12.2013 i.e. beyond the stipulated period of six months from dispossession.
Hence, Issue no 4a is hereby decided against the plaintiff.
VIII. RELIEF.
42. Ergo, in view of the above in extenso discussion, the suit of the plaintiff stands dismissed.
43. Decree sheet be prepared accordingly.
44. No order as to costs.
45. File be consigned to record room after necessary compliance.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
Further, the documents on which CS DJ 5568/2016 Page. 15 of 21 Mohd Akil Vs Yunus the plaintiff placed reliance on to establish possession, are mere photocopies and the said photocopies have not been proved as per the Indian Evidence Act.
32.Even if the claimant wanted to prove the existence and execution of a document by secondary evidence, it was first required of him to prove the existence of one of the several situations mentioned in Section 65 of the Evidence Act and thereafter to prove the document by secondary evidence of the form and the kind permitted in that situation.
Without fulfilling this twin task, no document can be said to have been proved by secondary evidence.
The claimant has failed to lead foundational evidence qua the fact that the originals are lost or destroyed etc before leading secondary evidence.
Thus, the person wanting to prove the existence and execution of a document by secondary evidence, before doing so, is first required to prove the existence of one of the several situations in which Section 65 permits proof of a document by secondary evidence and thereafter prove the document by secondary evidence of the form and the kind permitted in that situation.
Without fulfilling this twin task, no document can be said to have been proved by secondary evidence.
Such task can be performed only while leading evidence and the Court, only at the time of appreciating such evidence and which generally is at the time of final arguments, can hold whether a situation in which Section 65 permits secondary evidence has been proved to CS DJ 5568/2016 Page. 16 of 21 Mohd Akil Vs Yunus exist and if so, whether the document has been proved by secondary evidence.
No such finding can be returned on an application and without leading evidence.
The petitioner thus cannot take any advantage of the orders dated 22nd September, 2006 and 4th August, 2015 supra allowing the applications of the petitioner to prove the documents by secondary evidence.
In fact, the applications were misconceived as no permission for proof of a document by secondary evidence which is permitted by Evidence Act itself, is required.
Without the petitioner proving the existence of such situation, the question of proving the document by secondary evidence does not arise.
This is what is meant by "laying the foundation for leading secondary evidence".
34.
In the present case, the plaintiff has not been able to establish that the aforementioned documents are covered under the situations mentioned in Section 65 of the Indian Evidence Act.
